items.prompt: What is a rock, in geological terms?

options.label: Any solid object found on the ground
options.feedback: That includes things like broken bricks or dropped tools, which are not natural. A rock must occur naturally.

options.label: A single mineral crystal
options.feedback: A mineral is one crystalline substance, but a rock is usually an aggregate of many minerals or mineraloids.

options.label: A naturally occurring solid mass of minerals or mineraloid matter
options.feedback: Correct. A rock is natural, solid, and made of mineral or mineraloid grains.

options.label: A hard substance that contains metal
options.feedback: Rocks may contain metal-bearing minerals, but many rocks have no metal at all, and the definition does not require it.

items.ok_line: A rock is a natural solid mass of minerals or mineraloids.
items.ko_line: Reread what a rock actually is, not what it might look like.
items.exp_text: A rock is any naturally occurring solid mass made of minerals or mineraloid matter. It is not a single crystal, not something artificial, and not defined by containing metal.

items.prompt: Which three main groups are rocks usually divided into?

options.label: Igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic
options.feedback: Yes, those are the three great classes of rock.

options.label: Granite, basalt, limestone
options.feedback: Those are specific rock types, not the three main groups. Granite is igneous, basalt is igneous, limestone is sedimentary.

options.label: Crustal, mantle, core
options.feedback: Those are Earth's layers, not rock classes. Rocks can be found in all three groups regardless of where they sit.

options.label: Hard, soft, brittle
options.feedback: Those describe physical feel, not the geological classification based on how the rock formed.

items.ok_line: Igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic are the three main groups.
items.ko_line: These belong to a different system of grouping.
items.exp_text: Rocks are usually grouped into igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic. The group depends on how the rock formed, not on its hardness or where it sits in Earth.

options.label: By layers of sediment pressing together
options.feedback: That is how sedimentary rocks form, not igneous. Igneous rocks come from cooling magma or lava.

options.label: When magma or lava cools and solidifies
options.feedback: Correct. Cooling and solidification of molten rock produces igneous rocks.

options.label: When existing rock is squeezed by high pressure without melting
options.feedback: That describes metamorphism, not igneous formation. Metamorphic rocks transform from other rocks.

options.label: When tiny particles are glued together by minerals dissolved in water
options.feedback: That is cementation, part of sedimentary rock formation, not igneous.

items.ok_line: Cooling of magma or lava makes igneous rocks.
items.ko_line: That process belongs to another rock class.
items.exp_text: Igneous rocks form when molten rock, called magma underground or lava at the surface, cools and solidifies. The cooling can happen slowly in the crust or quickly on the surface.

items.prompt: What are the two main categories of igneous rocks?

options.label: Foliated and non-foliated
options.feedback: Those are categories of metamorphic rocks, based on texture. Igneous rocks are split by where they solidify.

options.label: Clastic and chemical
options.feedback: Those are types of sedimentary rocks, based on how particles or chemicals accumulate. Igneous rocks are not classified that way.

options.label: Intrusive and extrusive
options.feedback: That is correct! Plutonic (intrusive) and volcanic (extrusive) are the two categories.

options.label: Silicate and non-silicate
options.feedback: That is a mineral classification, not a division of igneous rock types. Most rocks contain silicates, but this is not the way igneous rocks are grouped.

items.ok_line: Plutonic/intrusive and volcanic/extrusive are the two main kinds.
items.ko_line: That grouping belongs to a different rock family.
items.exp_text: Igneous rocks split into plutonic (intrusive) rocks that cool slowly inside the crust, like granite, and volcanic (extrusive) rocks that cool at the surface, like basalt or pumice.

items.prompt: What is the original rock called before it undergoes metamorphism?

options.label: The magma
options.feedback: Magma is molten rock, not the original solid rock that gets transformed. The original rock is the protolith.

options.label: The sediment
options.feedback: Sediment is loose particles that may become sedimentary rock, not the starting rock for metamorphism. The starting rock is the protolith.

options.label: The protolith
options.feedback: Correct. The protolith is the original rock that changes into a metamorphic rock.

options.label: The country rock
options.feedback: Country rock is the rock that magma passes through as it rises, not the rock that becomes metamorphic.

items.ok_line: The protolith is the rock before metamorphism.
items.ko_line: That term refers to something else in geology.
items.exp_text: The original rock that gets transformed by heat and pressure is called the protolith. It can be igneous, sedimentary, or even an older metamorphic rock.

items.prompt: What do sedimentary rocks form from?

options.label: Accumulated and cemented fragments of older rocks, minerals, or organisms
options.feedback: Exactly. Sediments settle, compact, and cement into sedimentary rock.

options.label: Cooling of lava on the surface
options.feedback: That makes igneous rock, not sedimentary. Lava cooling forms basalt or pumice.

options.label: Direct transformation of solid rock by heat and pressure
options.feedback: That is metamorphism. Sedimentary rocks form by surface processes like deposition and cementation.

options.label: Crystallization of minerals from a cooling magma chamber
options.feedback: That is igneous formation. Sedimentary rocks do not come from magma.

items.ok_line: Sedimentary rocks come from cemented fragments and precipitates.
items.ko_line: That process creates a different rock class.
items.exp_text: Sedimentary rocks form at Earth's surface when fragments of older rocks or organic material settle and then get compacted and cemented, or when minerals precipitate from water.

items.prompt: What is the process called when existing rocks change into metamorphic rocks?

options.label: Diagenesis
options.feedback: Diagenesis is the compaction and cementation that forms sedimentary rocks, not the transformation that makes metamorphic rocks.

options.label: Metamorphism
options.feedback: Correct. Metamorphism means 'change in form' and turns any rock type into a metamorphic rock.

options.label: Lithification
options.feedback: Lithification is the process that turns loose sediment into solid sedimentary rock, not metamorphism.

options.label: Magma differentiation
options.feedback: That is a process in igneous magma, where magma changes composition as it rises, not a metamorphic process.

items.ok_line: Metamorphism is the transformation of rocks.
items.ko_line: That term belongs to a different rock-forming process.
items.exp_text: The transformation of any rock type into a metamorphic rock under different temperature and pressure is called metamorphism, meaning 'change in form'.

items.prompt: Which group of rocks often contains fossils?

options.label: Igneous rocks
options.feedback: Igneous rocks form from molten material, which would destroy any organism. Sedimentary rocks are the ones that preserve fossils.

options.label: Metamorphic rocks
options.feedback: Metamorphic rocks are altered by intense heat and pressure, which usually destroys fossils. Sedimentary rocks are the fossil-bearing ones.

options.label: Sedimentary rocks
options.feedback: Correct. Sedimentary rocks form from layers of sediment that can bury and preserve organisms.

options.label: All three groups equally
options.feedback: No, fossils are rarely preserved in igneous or metamorphic rocks; they are characteristic of sedimentary rocks.

items.ok_line: Sedimentary rocks are the ones that typically hold fossils.
items.exp_text: Sedimentary rocks often contain fossils because they accumulate from particles that can bury organisms. Igneous rocks form from molten material and metamorphic rocks are altered by high heat and pressure, both of which destroy fossils.

items.prompt: What is the term for rocks that form in horizontal layers or strata?

options.label: Igneous rocks
options.feedback: Igneous rocks can have layered flows, but the term 'stratified' specifically refers to sedimentary rocks laid down in layers.

options.label: Stratified rocks
options.feedback: Correct. Sedimentary rocks are often called stratified because they settle in horizontal or near-horizontal layers.

options.label: Metamorphic rocks
options.feedback: Metamorphic rocks may show foliation, but that is a different structure from sedimentary strata.

options.label: Mineraloids
options.feedback: Mineraloids are non-crystalline mineral-like substances, not layered rocks.

items.ko_line: That term refers to a specific layering in one rock group.
items.exp_text: Sedimentary rocks are frequently called stratified rocks because they form under gravity in horizontal or near-horizontal layers called strata.

options.label: Minerals that contain no oxygen
options.feedback: Silicate minerals contain silica tetrahedra, which include oxygen and silicon, so they do contain oxygen.

options.label: Minerals that are always black
options.feedback: Color is not part of the definition. Silicate minerals come in many colors, like quartz or feldspar.

options.label: Minerals that form only in metamorphic rocks
options.feedback: Silicate minerals are found in all rock types; they make up most of Earth's crust.

options.label: Minerals whose crystal structure includes silica tetrahedra
options.feedback: Correct. Silicate minerals have silica tetrahedra in their crystal lattice.

items.ok_line: Silicate minerals have silica tetrahedra in their structure.
items.ko_line: That description does not match silicate minerals.
items.exp_text: Silicate minerals are compounds that include silica tetrahedra in their crystal structure. They are the most common minerals, making up about 95% of Earth's crust.
